clue.text: Soldier and expert sharing a story

indicators.note: two words that share a letter let it be written once where they meet, so one copy drops out

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper
able means skilled or expert

explanation.surface: A soldier and a specialist swap tales.
explanation.walkthrough: PARA ends with A and ABLE starts with it, so the two words overlap on that one letter to make PARABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A parable is a short moral tale, so it is a kind of story.

clue.text: Thespian in role involving skill and sweat — but not in that order

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so the role word wraps around what follows

parts.note: an actor's part is a role
a trick is a knack or skill

indicators.note: the letters of the last word are to be rearranged rather than kept in their printed sequence

parts.note: the word as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor sweats away skilfully in a demanding role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But not in that order' looks like a comment on the sequence of skill and sweat, but it rearranges only the last word; both resulting pieces then sit together inside the role word, splitting it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick Stewart is an English stage and screen actor, Captain Picard in Star Trek, so he is an example of a thespian.

clue.text: Change verse after rock band left

parts.note: R.E.M. was an American rock band
an ode is a lyric poem
standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A poem gets rewritten once the rock group has departed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the verse behind the band, and 'left' then follows as a plain abbreviation rather than meaning departed.
explanation.definitionFit: To remodel something is to alter its structure or form, so it means to change.

clue.text: Member of parliament making old supporter fight

indicators.note: making one thing into another here means one letter is turned into a different piece

parts.note: a group of owls is called a parliament, so an owl is one of its members
standard abbreviation for old
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: An MP turns a former backer into a scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member of parliament' wants to be an MP; it is a bird, since a parliament is the collective noun for owls. Its O becomes BRA.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl is a rough, noisy fight, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Skinny latte at last — barely 14 litres!

indicators.note: barely suggests something stripped bare, so its outer letters are removed
at last points to the final letter only of the drink's name

parts.note: the final letter of latte
14 down is a superhero, and Spiderman is one
L is the abbreviation for litres

explanation.surface: A coffee-shop order: a skinny latte, but fourteen litres of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinny latte' reads as a low-fat coffee, but 'Skinny' is the definition, meaning to do with skin. The cross-reference to 14 needs an example of that answer, Spiderman, stripped of both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Epidermal means relating to the epidermis, the outer layer of skin, so the clue treats skinny playfully as 'of the skin'.

clue.text: Was silk a hard flipping thing to cut?

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it end to end, so the preceding string is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a silk is a senior barrister, a King's Counsel
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A question whether silk was a hard material to get through with scissors.
explanation.walkthrough: In the UK a senior barrister 'takes silk' and becomes a King's Counsel, KC. 'Flipping' could be an expletive but it reverses the whole run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw for metal, an implement one uses to cut, which the question mark flags as a loose description.

clue.text: Frequently visit hospital with relative

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital
an aunt is a family relation

explanation.surface: Someone keeps calling at the hospital alongside a family member.
explanation.definitionFit: To haunt a place is to go there habitually, so it means to visit often.

clue.text: Civil engineering outsourced for the most part

indicators.note: only most of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped
engineering something is building or contriving it, so the letters are put together in a new pattern

parts.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Most civil engineering work is contracted out to other firms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civil engineering' reads as one phrase but splits: 'Civil' is the definition and 'engineering' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Civil in the sense of polite: a courteous person shows good manners.

clue.text: Put small mollusc in sink deliberately

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a cuttle is a cuttlefish, a cephalopod mollusc

explanation.surface: Someone drops a little shellfish into the kitchen sink on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like a kitchen basin; it is a verb, and with 'deliberately' it defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To scuttle a ship is to sink it on purpose by holing it or opening its seacocks.

clue.text: Actor Martin Shaw filled in the middle somehow

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive in some unspecified new way, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the name as written

indicators.note: in the middle keeps only the central letters of the word just before it

parts.note: the four inner letters of filled

explanation.surface: Martin Shaw, star of The Professionals, somehow stepped in to fill a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: Martin Shaw is himself an English actor, which makes 'Actor Martin Shaw' read as one name; the definition is just 'Actor'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Shatner is the Canadian actor who played Captain Kirk in Star Trek, an instance of an actor.

clue.text: Curry maybe initially packed as needed in drums

parts.note: Tim Curry is an English actor, so Tim is one possible Curry

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the following words

parts.note: the first letters of packed, as, needed and in

explanation.surface: A curry is packed into tins as required.
explanation.definitionFit: Timpani are kettledrums, the tuned drums of an orchestra.

clue.text: Nancy's one regular drink — rum

parts.note: Nancy is a French city, and the French for one is un
'the usual' is the drink a pub regular always orders

explanation.surface: Nancy always drinks the same thing: rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink Nancy orders, but it is the old British adjective meaning odd. Nancy here is the city in north-east France, not a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is British informal for strange or peculiar, which is what unusual means.

clue.text: Dig tunnel out to be kind

indicators.note: out as in spread out or put out of place, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the two words as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to tunnel your way out, as an act of kindness.
explanation.definitionFit: An indulgent person is generous and lenient, readily granting what others want, so kind in that sense.

clue.text: African tour operator catching this on vacation

indicators.note: catching something means holding it, so the company name goes around the other piece

parts.note: TUI is a large European holiday company

indicators.note: a vacated word has been emptied, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of this

explanation.surface: An African travel firm takes this one on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like going on holiday, which suits a tour operator; it means the middle of 'this' is emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tutsi are an ethnic group of Rwanda and Burundi, so a Tutsi is an African.

clue.text: Wastes aptitude for cycling

indicators.note: cycling sends letters round in a loop, so the front letter moves to the back

parts.note: skill is a natural aptitude

explanation.surface: Someone squanders their talent for riding a bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aptitude for cycling' reads as a gift for bike riding; 'for cycling' is the signal to move SKILL's first letter to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang, to waste someone is to kill them, so wastes and kills are the same verb form.

clue.text: Hotel in Queens stopping work in lift — one with extraordinary power?

indicators.note: stopping a gap means plugging it, so this piece sits inside the next one
in a down clue a lift raises the word, so it reads from the bottom up

parts.note: an opus is a musical or literary work
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen; two of them for the plural
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A hotel in the New York borough of Queens has a broken lift, holding up work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queens' looks like the New York borough but means two monarchs, using the ER cipher of Elizabeth Regina, with the hotel letter between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A superhero is a fictional character with abilities beyond the ordinary; the question mark admits it is a description, not a dictionary gloss.

clue.text: Not a word about individual on gold monument

indicators.note: about means around, so the first piece wraps the others

parts.note: mum's the word: keeping mum is saying nothing

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is placed after it, so the word before this sends its piece second

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
sole means single or individual

explanation.surface: A gilded statue of a person, with no inscription at all.
explanation.walkthrough: As a command, 'mum' means stay silent, as in 'mum's the word'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mausoleum is a large stately tomb, a building raised as a memorial, so a kind of monument.

clue.text: Townsfolk turning TV on during a Belgium game

indicators.note: turning round makes the whole string run backwards, read up the down light

parts.note: a TV is a television set
in, as in 'in the night', means during
taken as written
B is Belgium's international vehicle code
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: Locals switch the TV on during a Belgium match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning TV on' reads as switching the set on; 'turning' actually reverses everything that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Urbanites are people who live in towns and cities, so the townsfolk.

clue.text: Reach singers getting to grips with tour where everything will be revealed

indicators.note: getting to grips with something means taking hold of it, so the band's name clasps the other piece

parts.note: Reach was a hit for the pop group S Club 7
a tour is a trip

explanation.surface: A pop group sets off on tour with a promise of full disclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reach' looks like a verb but is the 2000 single by S Club 7, the British pop group; their name minus the number wraps TRIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip club is a venue where performers undress, so it is cheekily described as a place where all is revealed.

clue.text: See 1
Tedious working life of shop people

parts.note: to shop and to rat both mean to inform on someone
a race is a people sharing descent

explanation.surface: The dull routine of retail workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shop people' reads as shop staff; 'shop' is the British slang verb meaning to betray to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the exhausting, competitive grind of modern working life.

clue.text: Mark Selby's source on which snooker balls might go

definitions.text: on which snooker balls might go

parts.note: a spot is a mark or stain

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of Selby

explanation.surface: Snooker player Mark Selby's beginnings at the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Selby is a world snooker champion, so 'Mark' looks like part of his name; it is a separate word giving SPOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Spots are the marked positions on a snooker table where coloured balls are placed or re-spotted.

clue.text: Doctor discovered locum on register

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its cover taken off, so the outer letters go

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters removed
a register is a list

explanation.surface: A medic finds a temporary GP's name on the official roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' reads as found, but splits as dis-covered, uncovered. 'On' in a down clue puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: An oculist is an old word for an eye doctor, a specialist in diseases of the eye.

clue.text: See 8
Carpenters' record

indicators.note: the possessive apostrophe signals the answer belongs to, and sits inside, the preceding word

parts.note: letters three to seven of the word

explanation.surface: A record by the Carpenters, the 1970s soft-rock duo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpenters' record' suggests an album by Karen and Richard Carpenter, but 'record' is a verb defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter data is to record it in a ledger or register.

clue.text: Writer finishing off prejudiced in Isle of Dogs for example

indicators.note: finishing off here means taking away the finish, so the last letter is lost

parts.note: a pen is a writing implement
insular means narrow-minded and prejudiced

explanation.surface: An author finishes off a bigoted piece in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Dogs is not an island but a loop of land in East London enclosed on three sides by the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A peninsula is land almost surrounded by water, and the Isle of Dogs is one such.

clue.text: Risk of salesman being upset with current line

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, which in a down clue turns the word bottom to top

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
I is the symbol for electric current
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A salesman, upset by the company's current policy, fears for his job.
explanation.definitionFit: Peril is serious danger, so it serves as a noun for risk.

clue.text: Face being under review every now and then

indicators.note: every now and then means occasionally, so only every other letter is read

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Someone's appearance is being reviewed from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' looks like a noun for the front of the head; here it means boldness.
explanation.definitionFit: Face as in 'to have the face to do something' means cheek or audacity, a synonym of nerve.

clue.text: A chess game's ending — you are caught being unprofessional

parts.note: taken as written
checkmate, shortened to mate, ends a game of chess

indicators.note: caught as in heard or picked up by ear, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: the letters U and R, said together, sound like the phrase

explanation.surface: A chess player is told they're caught out behaving unsportingly at the end of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateur as an adjective means unskilled or not done for pay, so unprofessional.

clue.text: Cast is not gathering in wings for Oliver Twist

indicators.note: gathering in means collecting something inside, so the rearranged letters surround another piece
to cast is to throw, and thrown letters land in a new arrangement

parts.note: the words as written

indicators.note: wings are the two sides of something, so the first and last letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of Oliver

explanation.surface: A theatre cast is not waiting in the wings for the musical Oliver! to start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oliver Twist' is the Dickens novel, which makes 'Twist' read as part of a title; it is the definition. 'Cast' and 'wings' both feel theatrical.
explanation.definitionFit: Torsion is the action of twisting, especially of one end of an object against the other.

clue.text: Litre of spread — possibly Clover

indicators.note: spread suggests the letters are scattered about and laid out again in a different order

parts.note: the two words as written

explanation.surface: A litre tub of spread, perhaps the Clover brand of butter substitute.
explanation.walkthrough: Clover is a British dairy spread brand, which is why its capital letter fits the surface; the plant clover is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trefoil is a plant with three-lobed leaves, and clover is the commonest example.

clue.text: Endure great heat in Jersey with area becoming essentially airless

indicators.note: becoming means turning into, so one letter changes into another

parts.note: a jersey is a knitted pullover
A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only the central letter is taken

parts.note: the central letter of airless

explanation.surface: Someone sweltering on the island of Jersey in a stuffy room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jersey' looks like the Channel Island; it is the garment, and its A turns into L.
explanation.definitionFit: To swelter is to be uncomfortably hot, suffering in oppressive heat.
